{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
{{For|a similar term|Negligible set}}

In mathematics, a '''negligible function''' is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}</math> such that for every positive [[integer]] ''c'' there exists an integer ''N''<sub>''c''</sub> such that for all ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''N''<sub>''c''</sub>,

:<math>|\mu(n)|<\frac{1}{n^c}.</math>

Equivalently, the following definition may be used.
A function <math>\mu:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is '''negligible''', if for every [[positive polynomial]] poly(·) there exists an integer ''N''<sub>poly</sub>&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 such that for all ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''N''<sub>poly</sub>

: <math>|\mu(n)|<\frac 1 {\operatorname{poly}(n)}.</math>

==History==
The concept of ''negligibility'' can find its trace back to sound models of analysis. Though the concepts of "[[continuous function|continuity]]" and "[[infinitesimal]]" became important in mathematics during [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] and [[Gottfried Leibniz|Leibniz]]'s time (1680s), they were not well-defined until the late 1810s. The first reasonably rigorous definition of ''continuity'' in [[mathematical analysis]] was due to [[Bernard Bolzano]], who wrote in 1817 the modern definition of continuity. Later [[Augustin Louis Cauchy|Cauchy]], [[Karl Weierstrass|Weierstrass]] and [[Eduard Heine|Heine]] also defined as follows (with all numbers in the [[real number]] domain <math>\mathbb{R}</math>):

:'''([[Continuous function]])''' A function <math>f:\mathbb{R}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{R}</math> is ''continuous'' at <math>x=x_0</math> if for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, there exists a positive number <math>\delta>0</math> such that <math>|x-x_0|<\delta</math> implies <math>|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon.</math>

This classic definition of continuity can be transformed into the definition of negligibility in a few steps by changing parameters used in the definition. First, in the case <math>x_0=\infty</math> with <math>f(x_0)=0</math>, we must define the concept of "''infinitesimal function''":

:'''([[Infinitesimal]])''' A continuous function <math>\mu:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is ''infinitesimal'' (as <math>x</math> goes to infinity) if for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there exists <math>N_\varepsilon</math> such that for all <math>x>N_\varepsilon</math>
::<math>|\mu(x)|<\varepsilon\,.</math>{{Citation needed|date=August 2007}}

Next, in the discrete setting where the domain is restricted to natural numbers <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math>, we replace <math>\varepsilon>0</math> by the functions <math>1/n^c</math> where <math>c>0</math> or by <math>1/\operatorname{poly}(n)</math> where <math>\operatorname{poly}(n)</math> is a positive [[polynomial]]. This leads to the definitions of negligible functions given at the top of this article. Since the constants <math>\varepsilon>0</math> can be expressed as <math>1/\operatorname{poly}(n)</math> with a constant polynomial, this shows that infinitesimal functions (restricted to <math>\mathbb{N}</math>) are a superset of negligible functions.

==Use in cryptography==

In complexity-based modern [[cryptography]], a security scheme is ''[[provable security|provably secure]]'' if the probability of security failure (e.g., inverting a [[one-way function]], distinguishing [[Cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator|cryptographically strong pseudorandom bits]] from truly random bits) is '''negligible''' in terms of the input security parameter or cryptographic key length <math>n</math>. Hence comes the definition at the top of the page because key length <math>n</math> must be a [[natural number]].

Nevertheless, the general notion of negligibility doesn't require that the input parameter <math>n</math> is strictly the key length. Indeed, <math>n</math> can be any predetermined discrete system metric and corresponding mathematical analysis would illustrate some hidden analytical behaviors of the system.

The reciprocal-of-polynomial formulation is used for the same reason that [[Computationally bounded adversary|computational boundedness]] is defined as polynomial running time: it has mathematical closure properties that make it tractable in the [[asymptotic security|asymptotic]] setting (see [[#Closure properties]]). For example, if an attack succeeds in violating a security condition only with negligible probability, and the attack is repeated a polynomial number of times, the success probability of the overall attack still remains negligible.

In practice one might want to have more [[concrete security|concrete]] functions bounding the adversary's success probability and to choose the [[security parameter]] large enough that this probability is smaller than some threshold, say&nbsp;2<sup>&minus;128</sup>.

==Closure properties==

One of the reasons that negligible functions are used in foundations of [[Computational complexity theory|complexity-theoretic]] cryptography is that they obey closure properties.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Introduction to modern cryptography|last=Katz|first=Johnathan|others=Lindell, Yehuda|date = 6 November 2014|isbn=9781466570269|edition= Second|location=Boca Raton|oclc=893721520}}</ref> Specifically,

# If <math>f,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}</math> are negligible, then the function <math>n\mapsto f(n)+g(n)</math> is negligible.
# If <math>f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is negligible and <math>p</math> is any real polynomial, then the function <math>n\mapsto p(n)\cdot f(n)</math> is negligible.

[[Converse (logic)|Conversely]], if <math>f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is not negligible, then neither is <math>n\mapsto f(n)/p(n)</math> for any real polynomial <math>p</math>.

==Examples==

{{Expand section|date=March 2018}}

* <math>n \mapsto a^{-n}</math> is negligible for any constant <math>a \geq 2</math>:
**   '''Step''': This is an [[exponential decay]] function where <math>a</math> is a constant greater than or equal to 2. As <math>n \to \infty</math>, <math>a^{-n} \to 0</math> very quickly, making it negligible.
* <math>f(n) = 3^{-\sqrt{n}}</math> is negligible:
**   '''Step''': This function has exponential decay with a base of 3, but the exponent grows slower than <math>n</math> (only at <math>\sqrt{n}</math>). As <math>n \to \infty</math>, <math>3^{-\sqrt{n}} \to 0</math>, so it’s still negligible but decays slower than <math>3^{-n}</math>.
* <math>f(n) = n^{-\log n}</math> is negligible:
**   '''Step''': In this case, <math>n^{-\log n}</math> represents a superpolynomial decay, with the exponent growing negatively due to <math>\log n</math>. Since the decay rate increases with <math>n</math>, the function goes to 0 faster than polynomial functions like <math>n^{-k}</math> for any constant <math>k</math>, making it negligible.
* <math>f(n) = (\log n)^{-\log n}</math> is negligible:
**   '''Step''': This function decays as the [[logarithm]] of <math>n</math> raised to a negative exponent <math>-\log n</math>, which leads to a fast approach to 0 as <math>n \to \infty</math>. The decay here is faster than inverse logarithmic or polynomial rates, making it negligible.
* <math>f(n) = 2^{-c \log n}</math> is not negligible, for positive <math>c</math>:
**   '''Step''': We can rewrite this as <math>f(n) = n^{-c}</math>, which is a polynomial decay rather than an exponential one. Since <math>c</math> is positive, <math>f(n) \to 0</math> as <math>n \to \infty</math>, but it doesn’t decay as quickly as true exponential functions with respect to <math>n</math>, making it non-negligible.

Assuming <math>n > 0</math> and a fixed real constant <math>a > 1</math>, we take the limit as <math>n \to \infty</math>:

'''Negligible:'''

* <math>f(n) = \frac{1}{a^{n/2}}</math>:
**   '''Step''': This function decays exponentially with base <math>a</math> raised to the power of <math>-\frac{n}{2}</math>. As <math>n \to \infty</math>, <math>a^{-\frac{n}{2}} \to 0</math> quickly, making it negligible.
* <math>f(n) = \frac{1}{a^{\log{(n^k)}}}</math> for <math>k \geq 1</math>:
**   '''Step''': We can simplify <math>a^{-\log(n^k)}</math> as <math>n^{-k \log a}</math>, which decays faster than any polynomial. As <math>n \to \infty</math>, the function approaches zero and is considered negligible for any <math>k \geq 1</math> and <math>a > 1</math>.
* <math>f(n) = \frac{1}{a^{(\log n)^k}}</math> for <math>k \geq 1</math>:
**   '''Step''': The decay is determined by the base <math>a</math> raised to the power of <math>-(\log n)^k</math>. Since <math>(\log n)^k</math> grows with <math>n</math>, this function approaches zero faster than polynomial decay, making it negligible.
* <math>f(n) = \frac{1}{a^{\sqrt{n}}}</math>:
**   '''Step''': Here, <math>f(n)</math> decays exponentially with a base of <math>a</math> raised to <math>-\sqrt{n}</math>. As <math>n \to \infty</math>, <math>f(n) \to 0</math> quickly, so it’s considered negligible.
* <math>f(n) = \frac{1}{a^{n(\log n)}}</math>:
**   '''Step''': With an exponential base and exponent <math>n(\log n)</math>, this function would approach zero very rapidly, suggesting negligibility.

'''Non-negligible:'''

* <math>f(n) = \frac{1}{n^{1/n}}</math>:
**   '''Step''': Since <math>n^{1/n} \to 1</math> as <math>n \to \infty</math>, this function decays very slowly, failing to approach zero quickly enough to be considered negligible.
